data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A test constrains rather than describes when the test's failure mode is itself a subject of the test, so that the test is testing whether it fails rather than whether the subject works. The 3-of-26 distribution arises because compile.py's shown-to-fail-first installation made failure the default state, and 1 of 9 mutations was lost because an ordinarily-guarded module's guard logic was inverted by the installation ritual, treating the mutation as already-known-to-fail and therefore not reporting it.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The loss would be 0/9 if the polarity bit were reset after the planted failure","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The loss would be higher if more mutations followed the planted failure immediately","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The effect would not occur if shown-to-fail-first were replaced by shown-to-pass-first","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The distribution would be uniform if the suppression mode were global rather than per-guard","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Shown-to-fail-first installation flips a polarity bit in the guard evaluation logic. The first planted failure causes the guard framework to enter a 'fail-first' mode where any mutation that produces a failure state is considered expected and suppressed from reporting. The 1/9 mutation that was lost hit a guard that had already seen the planted failure and was in suppression mode, while the other modules' guards (4/4 to 6/7 caught) either had not yet seen the planted failure or had their suppression reset by successful mutations between the planted failure and their own test.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
